@@135549948 <h> New albums from avant-garde pop artists Fcukers and Slayyyter aggressively embrace hedonism in a world of emotional dysregulation and assaulting news . By Shaad D'Souza . <h> Two new albums for dancing in the dark times <p> Something interesting happened on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon a couple of weeks back . Fallon introduced a band called , in his TV-friendly version , " eff-see-you-kay-ers " . The screen faded to a painfully trendy scene : a band of gorgeous people playing a pounding pop-techno track , its vocal provided by a disaffectedly cool girl in sunnies and a black skivvy . Behind the band a bunch of hot extras swayed around aimlessly , as if they had accidentally wandered onto the Fallon set and it was the least cool party they had been to that night . <p> The song is called " I Like It Like That " and it 's by the band Fcukers -- actually pronounced " Fuckers " -- a New York-based duo made up of producer Jackson Walker Lewis and singer Shanny Wise . The fact Fallon was forced to bowdlerise the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ booking . Fcukers is a band practically designed to radiate underground cool and here they were on one of television 's biggest possible artist bookings , forcing Fallon -- who seems to struggle with uncommon words on a good day -- to break out the phonetics . <p> " I Like It Like That " is taken from ? , Fcukers ' debut album , set for release this month on the venerated electronic label Ninja Tune . It is a loud , sexy , hedonistic record that brings to mind the fuck-it-let's-party ethos of the late 2000s and early 2010s . Throughout , Lewis and Wise create the feeling that partying can , and should , be totalising and dissociative . Wise sings in the same whispery deadpan throughout , as if her conscious flattening is not just an affect but a lifeline in a time when emotional dysregulation has become a norm thanks to TikTok , and as the news has become increasingly assaultive . <p> It 's showcased in a glamorous and raucous package , adopting a structure that Lady Gaga described a few years ago as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a very good record if you take Fcukers on their own terms : this stuff is n't that serious , nor should it be . Although I do find the critical idea that some records are " for " some people and " not for " others horribly asinine -- " It 's just not for me " is usually a way to absolve oneself of any critical thinking -- I suspect this will be an album that is specifically for those who like to go out and obliterate their every last brain cell every other weekend and specifically disliked by those who do n't . <p> These records are about enjoying your life now , despite the moment -- or , perhaps , because of it . <p> Fcukers have taken an unusual path to prospective stardom . Both members used to be in indie bands : Lewis in a group called Spud Cannon and Wise in a vintage-toned duo named The Shacks . At one point they had a third member , Ben Scharf , who was in Spud Cannon with Lewis . He has since left the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not talk about him in their interviews . Spud Cannon and The Shacks were vestiges of an older , more earnest kind of indie music that prized aesthetic and persona but purported not to . Now the scene is much more diffuse , less of a pipeline to any kind of real stardom and hardly appropriate for two obvious stars like Fcukers . <p> The pair met when both were working in hospitality in New York , Wise running a restaurant named Betty with her then best friend , Lewis working at the famed dive bar Pianos . By Leila Lois . <h> Traditions merge in the visionary Flora <p> Flora , the first full-length collaboration between The Australian Ballet and Bangarra Dance Theatre , is a brave work that will touch audiences hungry for celebrations of unity and collective dreaming through art . <p> There are few art forms that can close the perceived gap between people of different backgrounds and people and " nature " as effectively as dance , which demands , as a very proviso of engagement , bodily contact and the holding of space . This year Bangarra won the Venice Biennale 's Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement in Dance -- the first Australian company to do so -- which honours the company 's power to portray important truths to audiences who need to witness them , in exceptionally resonant and technically brilliant ways . <p> Flora echoes Robin Wall Kimmerer 's influential book Braiding Sweetgrass . Kimmerer weaves together Indigenous ( Potawatomi ) wisdom and Western botanical science to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ deserving of gratitude and reciprocity . Both Kimmerer and Rings perceive the urgency of the grammar of animacy in action : the land , the plants , the knowledge are not backdrops but presences that must be properly addressed . <p> Both artistic directors -- The Australian Ballet 's David Hallberg and Rings -- have remarked on the sense of unity that unfolded in rehearsals . The dancers themselves referred to the season as the " Flora Ensemble " , a new company in sentiment and impetus that takes the knowledge and groundedness of Indigenous dance and allows space for ballet to breathe into this practice on Indigenous land . <p> It feels visionary and unique -- the distinctiveness in training and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ collaboration to pure presence in Rings 's work , which demands rootedness and authenticity . By Jacinta Parsons . <h> Barry Jones 's talkback scrapbook <p> In a recent interview with David Marr on ABC Radio National , Barry Jones , perhaps unintentionally , summed up his life 's work : " I 'm obsessive about changing the world , about doing good stuff , about forcing people to think more creatively , more imaginatively , more courageously ... with the various clocks ticking toward midnight , we 're not delivering as we should be . " <p> It 's an urgent message from a man who is very aware of the march of time . At 93 , Jones continues to plead for public engagement in meaningful conversation . Within a day of each other , Mike Walsh on 2SM in Sydney and Barry Jones on 3DB in Melbourne hosted the very first iterations in their respective cities . <p> Jones had come to national public attention as the champion of the GTV-9 Melbourne television quiz program Pick a Box . @@135552355 <p> London/Dubai : In the arid heart of the Arabian Peninsula , where scorching temperatures and negligible rainfall define the landscape , water is not merely a resource ; it is the linchpin of survival . <p> The six member states of the Gulf Co-operation Council ( GCC ) -- Saudi Arabia , the United Arab Emirates , Kuwait , Bahrain , Qatar and Oman -- rely overwhelmingly on desalination plants to quench their thirst . These facilities , which convert seawater into potable supplies , provide most of the drinking water for populations that have ballooned amid oil-driven prosperity . <p> The Persian Gulf relies on nearly 450 facilities to turn seawater into drinking water . They are now under threat.AFP <p> Iran 's ability to strike the GCC 's desalination plants , whether with missiles , drones , small boat swarms or cyberattacks , poses an existential threat to these six Arab states . Unlike the GCC nations , Iran draws most of its water from rivers , reservoirs and aquifers , with desalination accounting for about 2 per cent of its supply . <p> Advertisement <p> While @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the GCC states could face rapid societal collapse without theirs . Saudi Arabia , the regional powerhouse , derives about 70 per cent of its drinking water from desalinated sources . Collectively , the GCC produces 40 per cent of the world 's desalinated water , operating more than 400 plants that transform the saline Persian Gulf into a lifeline . <h> Related Article <p> This vulnerability stems from decades of rapid urbanisation and industrial growth , fuelled by hydrocarbon wealth but constrained by nature 's parsimony . @@135576500 <p> National security in Australia has long seemed an elite endeavour -- kept apart from the public through the coded language of experts , bureaucrats and don't-rock-the-boat politics . That was never exactly democratic and it just wo n't work any more in a new world of cascading shocks that affect us all . <p> Comprehensive new evidence shows that most Australians are worried about security , see multiple looming risks , and think the nation is underprepared . <p> Our recent surveys show that large majorities , between 72 and 78 per cent of the population , perceive the following issues as serious concerns over the next decade : cyber threats , AI-enabled attacks , terrorism , violent extremism , economic crisis , supply-chain disruption , disinformation , foreign interference and the failure of the global rules-based order . <p> In recognising this new world of risk , people also want government to tell them more about what is going on . So , what do Australians really think about our nation 's security in this new world of risk ? <p> Citizens have shown strategic judgment on everything from community cohesion to military threats , foreign interference to climate change , terrorism to disinformation , the downsides of AI to the risks -- now the reality -- of crisis in our economic supply chains . <p> Their views include plenty of commonsense and logical analysis about sensitive security issues , where the risk-averse option for governments of all persuasions has often been to give @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ conversation . <p> The bad news -- which the nation needs to confront with honesty -- is that public anxiety is rising across a wide spectrum of issues . In every case other than military attack , more than two-thirds considered the risk more likely than not to " happen as a threat to Australia " within five years . In six cases -- climate change impacts , AI-enabled attacks , disinformation , foreign interference , economic crisis and critical supply disruption -- the proportion that considered the threat more likely than not was between 85 and 89 per cent . @@135577583 <p> If it wants stable gas supply and lower gas prices , the federal government needs to be adaptive and flexible in reserving domestic gas production for domestic users . Otherwise , domestic manufacturing will wither . <p> Three things in life are certain : death , taxes , and a jump in oil and gas prices whenever there 's geopolitical conflict . <p> Thanks to the US -- Iran conflict , the Strait of Hormuz is effectively closed , and 25 percent of the world 's liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) trade is cut off . The LNG benchmark price for Japan and South Korea jumped in response to the initial closure , from about US$10.70 ( about A$15 ) to more than US$15 ( about A$21 ) . And it jumped again following missile strikes on Qatar 's biggest LNG facility , to more than US$22 ( about A$31 ) . <p> Because Australia is a big exporter of gas , this price ( and the jump ) flows through to the Australian economy . It affects electricity prices , domestic gas prices , and , through @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to domestic manufacturing , including manufacturing that 's essential to national resilience in the face of security threats . <p> Stand by for a repeat of the effects of the Russia -- Ukraine war : higher gas prices , higher electricity prices , higher inflation , a higher cost of living , and more domestic manufacturers unable to stay in business . <p> Successive federal governments have tried for years to break the link between world and domestic gas prices . Complicating matters on the east coast , gas fields in Victoria are starting to run dry , raising the real prospect of gas shortages in coming years . <p> Late last year , the federal government admitted it was time for wholesale reform , and it is now designing a domestic gas reservation . <p> The government 's stated intention is to make gas exporters supply the domestic market first , before they can export . This should give the domestic market more gas than it needs so that prices fall on average and there 's a buffer if international prices spike . <p> The government says exporters wo @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ already signed . This creates a tricky design problem , and the simplest answers are not the ones that deliver the results the government wants . <p> The simplest design that comes to mind is to take a portion of the spot cargoes -- the gas that is n't exported under a contract and is currently being sold at wartime-high prices . <p> This is what the gas producers want . But it will lead to disappointing results for domestic gas users and leave the link to international prices unchanged . The volume of spot cargoes is small compared to domestic demand . Just targeting these will mean significant volumes of gas wo n't be delivered to the domestic market until the mid-2030s , by which time distressed manufacturers would have closed down , and the remaining ones would be switching over to using electricity where they can . <p> At the Grattan Institute , we 've identified two key decisions the government needs to get right : <p> -- How much extra gas does the government want supplied to the domestic market ? <p> -- How will the government @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ extra gas that closes supply gaps and keeps downward pressure on prices is going to vary from year to year . Demand for gas is inherently unpredictable , though it is generally trending downwards . <p> In our proposed model , the government would use its forecasts of domestic supply and domestic demand to work out how much extra gas is required for the coming year . In 2029 ( the year supply gaps first appear ) , only 3 petajoules will be needed to avoid shortages . In 2032 , it 's more like 50 petajoules . <p> The government could then allocate the obligation to supply this extra gas across the exporters by applying a percentage proportional to how much LNG they are planning to produce and export . It 's critical that this is based on all planned exports , not just spot cargoes , because , as noted above , the spot cargoes do n't provide enough gas . <p> Once the amount of gas had been divvied up between exporters , it would then be up to each exporter to figure out how they get @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ cargoes , increase production or pay another domestic producer to increase production on its behalf . Exporters could also choose to divert gas from an existing contract , with the other party 's consent . <p> To give certainty to exporters so they can sign long-term contracts , the percentage used to divide the obligation should have a ceiling on it -- we suggest 15 percent of all exports . But underneath that ceiling , it should fluctuate to reflect how much gas the domestic market requires . <p> Under our model , everyone gets what they need . The exporters have certainty that there 's a ceiling on their obligations . The domestic market has a steady supply of gas that matches demand and puts downward pressure on prices , helping households and manufacturers . Domestic producers know there 's a limit on how much competition they face from government-mandated supply . And the government can relax a little when the next geopolitical conflict comes along . <p> Author <p> Alison Reeve is director of the Energy and Climate Change Program at the Grattan Institute .

@@135665822 <p> The world 's largest carbon emitters owe a huge debt to future generations . Some experts say that debt can be quantified financially . <p> That 's largely because the negative impacts of climate change wo n't fall proportionally to responsibility . Some of the countries most likely to be hit dramatically by the adverse effects of climate change , such as small island nations facing the threat of completely losing their land to rising sea levels , have historic emission contributions that are dwarfed by those of top emitters like the United States . <p> In a new study , researchers at Stanford developed a quantitative framework to link individual emissions to actual damages that have happened and will happen around the globe . The framework is based on an estimate linking warming temperatures to the GDP of each country , offering a glimpse into the impact climate change is having on our world . The actual impact is likely much more significant since the data does n't account for areas that are " poorly captured in GDP data , " the researchers said , like climate-related health @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> According to findings published in Nature on Wednesday , the United States has already caused $10 trillion in global damages from carbon emissions since 1990 . Specifically , the researchers were able to link U.S. emissions since 1990 with $500 billion of damage in India , $330 billion in Brazil , and $1.39 trillion in the European Union . The United States ' carbon footprint also took a heavy toll on the nation itself . The researchers estimated that the U.S. has suffered a $16.2 trillion hit from all global carbon emissions since 1990 , with $2.97 trillion of this damage stemming directly from American carbon emissions . <p> Here 's the real kicker , though : past emissions not only continue to cause future damages , but those future costs will also be 10 times higher than the past damages from those same emissions , the researchers estimate . So , for example , one metric ton of carbon emitted in 1990 caused an estimated $180 in global damages by the year 2020 , the researchers say , and will continue to cause $1,840 in damages through 2100 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will not settle debts for past emissions , " the researchers conclude in the study . <p> The study used the framework to illustrate the debts of individual actions , too . For example , emissions from private flights taken in 2022 by Bill Gates , Elon Musk , Jeff Bezos , Jay-Z , and Taylor Swift will each cause more than $1 million in damages by 2100 . In contrast , if you took a single long-haul flight per year over the last decade , then chances are your carbon footprint from that action will lead to roughly $25,000 in future damages by 2100 , the study finds . <p> So individual actions have tangible consequences , but the good news is that it goes both ways . So , on the flip side , switching to a vegetarian diet or reducing your driving by 10% would each result in $6,000 of reduced future damages if you do them for a decade . Even if you were to cut down on your beef consumption by eating one less serving per month over a decade , that would generate at @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ effect might not seem as large , sadly , as the impact the biggest polluters are having on the economy , but it is a place to start . There is a " lasting global impact of even relatively small changes in individual behavior , " the researchers conclude . <p> As for settling any debt by larger institutions , direct financial compensation is the most practical approach for addressing past damages , the researchers say . Despite its pitfalls -- such as deciding which households deserve the money versus who actually receives it -- it remains the most workable option . This framework could be a starting point for figuring that out , but the researchers note that absolute damages do n't necessarily indicate what is actually owed to each economy by other emitters . <p> " For example , we compute that the damages experienced by the US from global emissions since 1990 are greater than the global damages caused by the US by its own emissions over that period , but this need not imply that a framework for responsibility would necessarily assign the US to be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> But even when you settle up past debts , the past emissions continue to impact people around the world . For compensating future debt , the best method is to limit the damage . <p> Carbon removal technologies could be a solution , but even that has limitations . Besides the fact that the technology in its current form is usually expensive and energy-intensive , its effectiveness at preventing future damage diminishes if the carbon is not removed immediately upon its emission . So immediate carbon removal would eliminate all damages , but a 25-year delay would only result in a 50% reduction in damages , the researchers say . <p> Ultimately , the best way to combat future damage is to just produce less carbon dioxide , it seems . But the hot air is on the move . <p> The reason these high temperatures persist is the " heat dome " phenomenon , in which high pressure prevents hot air from rising , trapping it in a bubble above a region . As the dome of pressure moves , so too does the hot air -- and right now , it 's barreling east . <p> The states that will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ include those in the Southern and Central Plains regions . As humidity can contribute to dehydration , body strain and breathing difficulties , lower humidity makes this heat dome somewhat less dangerous for workers in affected areas . <p> The World Weather Attribution , an initiative formed by international climate change researchers and climate scientists , determined that the heat dome would be " virtually impossible without human-induced climate change . " <p> In a world where weather events like these cease to be impossibilities , you 'll want to prepare for future heat waves properly . These HVAC system additions are extremely energy efficient , which means you can keep more money in your pocket while beating the heat . <p> During the middle of the heat wave , when everyone has their AC running , there 's also the potential for an early brownout ( a temporary drop in electrical voltage , causing lighting to dim ) or even a blackout ( a complete loss of power ) . It 's common to feel helpless during power outages , but you can get ahead of the curve by preparing a summer blackout kit with portable chargers and alternative light sources before the heat wave hits . <p> Even if the historic heat wave does n't hit your home , these tips will help you prepare as the summer season bears down on the US in a couple of months . 
@@135666430 <p> The Strait of Hormuz is far from Australia , but in every energy crisis there is a reminder that energy security is not currently measured by how much sun a country has falling on rooftops . It is measured by what keeps moving when oil markets seize up , shipping insurance rates spike , or refined fuel cargoes get repriced in a week . <p> Australia likes to describe itself as a renewable energy superpower in waiting , and on electricity supply potential that is fair enough . But the country still runs a large share of its economy , and especially its mobility , on imported liquid fuels exposed to global chokepoints . <p> The lesson from Hormuz is not that Australia needs a new panic plan for the Gulf . It is that the country needs to get serious about electrifying the parts of its economy that remain tied to traded oil . <p> Richard Rumelt 's kernel of good strategy is useful here because it forces discipline . Diagnosis comes first . Then guiding policy . Then coherent actions . Australia has spent years discussing electrification @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ batteries , tariffs , and standards as if they were all equivalent pieces of a buffet . They are not . <p> The diagnosis is that Australia is behind on economy-wide electrification . The guiding policy should be to accelerate electrification where it is commercially ready and strategically important . The coherent actions should start with the measures Australia can control directly , rather than the technologies it can only encourage from a distance . <p> On the diagnosis , the numbers are plain . The Department of Climate Change , Energy , the Environment and Water 's Australian Energy Flows for 2023-24 shows final energy consumption of about 1,121 TWh , of which only about 241 TWh was electricity . <p> That means Australia is only about 21.5% electrified on a final energy basis . The rest is still mostly oil , gas , and smaller amounts of coal and other fuels . Oil alone accounted for about 654 TWh of final consumption . <p> This is the reality hidden behind the solar success story . Australia has done a great deal on renewable electricity generation , but it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ end uses . The country is not failing to build electrons . It is lagging on using them to displace molecules . <p> Australia 's formal organizations are all in petajoules ( PJ ) , but I choose to express energy in its final , dominant expression , units of electricity . Electricity is billed , planned , modeled , and debated in kWh , MWh , GWh , and TWh . PJ is useful in national energy statistics because it lets coal , oil , gas , and electricity all sit in one accounting frame . <p> But it obscures the practical question : How much electricity would Australia need to replace fossil energy services , and where is it being used now ? TWh is the more intuitive unit for that conversation . One TWh is 3.6 PJ . Once the article turns from aggregate fuel accounting to strategy , TWh makes the scale of the problem easier to see . <p> The transport data make the point sharper . Transport consumed about 489 TWh of final energy in 2023-24 , and only about 7.2 TWh of that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ words , the biggest block of final energy in the economy remains barely electrified . <p> Residential is already much further along , with about 70 TWh of electricity out of about 133 TWh of final energy . Commercial is further still , with about 64 TWh of electricity out of about 87 TWh . In large part that 's due to Australia being a sunburnt country that needs more cooling than heating . <p> Manufacturing and mining are lower than buildings , but both are still substantially ahead of transport . If the objective is to move the national electrification needle in the late 2020s and early 2030s , passenger road transport is the obvious place to focus . This is not because industry , freight , or buildings do not matter . It is because road transport is where the largest unelectrified energy block overlaps with a mature and scaling technology path . <p> That strategic focus looks even stronger through a useful energy lens . Australia 's TWh energy flow Sankey diagrams make the core point well . Australia uses far more input energy than it needs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ much energy as heat . <p> Internal combustion vehicles are a clean example . A battery electric vehicle commonly turns 70% to 80% of the electricity stored in the battery into motion at the wheels . A gasoline vehicle often turns only 20% to 25% of the fuel 's energy into motion , with the rest lost as heat . Even if one stays away from exact one-for-one comparisons across driving cycles , the order of magnitude is not controversial . <p> Replacing combustion in passenger transport is not just fuel switching . It is a large efficiency gain . That is why electrification can cut total energy demand while improving the same energy services . <p> Australia is well placed to benefit from that in a way many countries are not . The country has built one of the world 's largest distributed solar fleets . The national CER roadmap says Australia reached its 4 millionth rooftop solar system in December 2024 , average rooftop system size reached 9.9 kW in the first quarter of 2025 , and smart meter coverage reached 60% of National Electricity Market customers . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ risen to 4.3 million households by the end of 2025 , with 28.3 GW of installed capacity . Australia does not have a lack of midday electricity in many places . <p> It increasingly has a challenge of using that electricity productively and then managing the late afternoon and evening when rooftop solar output falls away . That is why the first and biggest grid value from electric vehicles is not glamorous . It is demand management . <p> Growth of EV Battery Exploitation Strategies by author <p> This is the point many discussions still miss . The first systemic prize from millions of EVs is not that they can discharge to the grid . It is that they do not have to charge at the wrong time . <p> AEMO 's 2025 Electricity Statement of Opportunities for the NEM and the parallel WEM outlook for Western Australia both point to the same broad pattern . Peak stress is increasingly in the late afternoon and evening , after solar generation fades , and in Western Australia the peak is extending later into the night . <p> That means badly timed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ EV charging can help solve it . A car that simply waits until after the evening peak , or better yet charges during a midday solar soak window , is already providing system value . No bidirectional power flow is required . No export settlement is required . No debate about battery warranty is required . The charger just needs to be smart enough , and the tariff or control signal clear enough , to avoid charging at the wrong time . <p> That makes demand managed charging the highest value proposition for Australia in the near term . It is the part of the solution that the country can influence most directly . Distribution businesses and regulators already shape tariff structures through Tariff Structure Statements approved by the Australian Energy Regulator . <p> The AER 's own work on facilitating consumer energy resources points directly to time of use tariffs and solar soak periods as ways to steer EV charging into times when distributed solar is abundant . <p> Network proposals in Victoria are already moving in that direction . CitiPower 's tariff proposals reference an 11 a.m. to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to time of use pricing by shifting away from peak . Jemena has proposed a default residential time of use tariff with a daytime solar soak component . This is the sort of thing Australia can do with its own institutions , its own rules , and its own retailers . <p> As Daniel Kahneman argued in the work that led to his 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics , people do not approach choices as frictionless optimisers . They rely on fast intuitive judgment , are loss averse , and show a strong bias toward the status quo . <p> In his Nobel autobiographical essay , Kahneman said loss aversion was central because people respond more strongly to losses than equivalent gains , and that this helps explain a widespread bias favoring the status quo in decision making . <p> Applied to EV charging , that means a complicated mandatory time of use tariff asks households to study unfamiliar rules , trust that they will not be penalized , and actively change established behavior , all of which feels like risk and effort . A default smart charging profile does @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ beneficial behavior automatic , while preserving the option to override it . <p> Behavioral economics and cognitive science both suggest that when a policy depends on millions of households making repeated complex decisions under uncertainty , adoption will be weaker than when the system quietly makes the low-cost , low-risk choice the default . <p> There is an important nuance here . Australia can do more with opt out or default smart charging than with universal mandatory time of use billing in the near term . Most consumers do n't understand dynamic tariff structures . Not every consumer trusts them . Some will be worse off if poorly designed tariffs shift risk onto households that do not have flexibility . But an EV charger does not need the owner to become a part time energy trader . <p> It can come with a default profile that delays charging out of the evening peak unless the driver overrides it . A retailer can offer an EV charging product with a simple off peak default and a visible price advantage . <p> A network can create the framework for dynamic EV charger @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The strategic insight is simple . Consumers should have to opt out of good charging behavior , not opt in after reading a small thesis on network pricing . <p> If demand management is the first value proposition , vehicle to home is the second . Australia has a housing stock and consumer energy stack that make V2H more plausible than in most jurisdictions . According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics , 72.3% of occupied private dwellings are separate houses . Car ownership is high . Owner occupation is high . Rooftop solar penetration is high . <p> The federal government 's V2X ( vehicle-to-any ) guidance notes that V2H can reduce home energy costs during peak times and reduce reliance on the grid when it is constrained . <p> That is a logical fit with Australian housing . A household with a detached home , driveway , rooftop solar , and an EV parked at home in the evening has a clean use case . The car can absorb midday solar or off peak electricity and then cover part of the late afternoon and evening household load . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to understand than exporting back through market arrangements to support the wider grid . As I 've noted a couple of times , it 's much more aligned with Kahneman 's prospect theory insights than vehicle-to-grid 's ( V2G ) value propositions . <p> But V2H has headwinds , and they are not trivial . The federal government says that currently very few EVs in Australia have V2X capability confirmed by the vehicle manufacturer . <p> That is a blunt statement , and it matters . It means the household case may be attractive , but the product market is immature . There are also charger costs , interoperability concerns , installation requirements , and battery warranty questions . <p> The Arena and RACE for 2030 National Roadmap for Bidirectional EV Charging is useful partly because it admits , in polite language , how early the market still is . It is a roadmap to commercial adoption , not a review of a mature mass market . <p> It also notes that certification processes under the latest standards were still untested and that this creates a risk reward tradeoff for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ market is not ready for rapid mainstream takeoff . <p> That is why V2G sits third in the sequence . This does not mean V2G lacks value . It means it requires more moving parts and more maturity . A V2G proposition needs compatible vehicles , compatible chargers , standards alignment , certification , network permissions , retailer arrangements , communications standards , aggregation logic , and consumer confidence that the car will still be charged when needed and that the battery warranty will still hold . <p> It is notable and in my opinion incorrect that ARENA 's roadmap emphasizes V2G as the highest value and most scalable bidirectional use case and targets 300,000 V2G capable EVs by 2030 . The practical reading is not that V2G is about to become the defining feature of Australian EV ownership . It is that institutions are trying to lay the groundwork for a later stage of market development , and possibly missing the forest for the trees . <p> This is where the distinction between what Australia can control and what it can not becomes decisive . Australia can influence tariff @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ installation standards , charger communications , retailer product design , and fleet procurement . It has policy leverage there . It has very limited leverage over global automakers ' product roadmaps . <p> Australia is a small global vehicle market , around 1% to 1.2% of global new vehicle sales , and it is a minority right hand drive market . That matters . A country of that size can shape the conditions under which charging happens . <p> Australia can not force automotive original equipment manufacturers to prioritise bidirectional capability for consumers if they see higher priority markets elsewhere . It can help make Australia an easier and more profitable market to serve . It can not dictate global platform decisions . <p> That points to a clean policy sequence . First , make demand managed charging normal . Require that new chargers supported through public incentives or retailer programs be smart chargers capable of responding to time based and dynamic signals . Require default charging profiles that avoid the evening peak and favor overnight and solar soak windows . <p> Standardise communication requirements so chargers can participate in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ work on EVSE technical standards and service and installation rules . Expand smart meter coverage and data access where it is still thin . <p> Use fleet procurement , workplaces , and apartment charging programs to build large pools of controllable load . None of that depends on waiting for global OEMs to include standardized bidirectional charging at scale . <p> Australia can change how chargers deliver electricity to cars much more easily than it can make global EV OEMs build cars to Australian desires . <p> Second , prepare the market for V2H without pretending it is already a mass market . Australia should keep reducing standards friction , support charger certification , and make sure home energy management systems can integrate rooftop solar , batteries , and EVs cleanly . <p> It should focus on the near term consumer story that makes sense . Use your own solar better . Reduce your evening imports . Have a household backup option where appropriate . That is easier to sell , easier to understand , and easier to regulate than early stage V2G participation across a fragmented retail market . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ pathway , but do not let it dominate the 2020s policy agenda . V2G may become important , especially as EV fleets become larger , standards settle , and interoperable products become common . It may well be part of the 2030s and 2040s system architecture . But a strategy built around near term V2G scale would be a strategy built around the least mature piece of the stack . Rumelt would call that bad strategy . It mistakes an interesting possibility for a leverage point . <p> What should Australia do if it wants a coherent and effective strategy rather than a technology shopping list ? <p> Start with the oil problem exposed by Hormuz . Passenger road transport is the most exposed and least electrified major energy use . Make EV adoption the central transport electrification priority . Then treat those EVs first as flexible demand . <p> Build opt-out smart charging into the market as the default behavior . Make smart chargers a near term must have for new dedicated home charging . Shape tariffs and retailer offers so that cheap midday and overnight charging becomes the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ value proposition where the housing stock and consumer economics fit . Keep working on V2G standards and pilots , but do not confuse preparation with immediate scale . <p> If Australia gets this right , the gains come from several directions at once . Household fuel bills fall because electricity displaces imported oil . Grid costs are reduced because EV load shifts away from the hours when the system is under most pressure . Rooftop solar gets used more productively . The national electrification rate starts moving upward faster because the largest fossil fuel demand block finally begins to convert . <p> Every increase in electric kilometers driven reduces the economy 's exposure to events in places like Hormuz . That is the strategy . Not gadgetry . Not technology tourism . @@135696824 <p> The new film adaptation of Enid Blyton 's The Magic Faraway Tree is daggy . That uniquely antipodean adjective , at once derisive and affectionate , best sums up the film itself and the original books that inspired it . <p> I do n't think I can recommend the film itself with a straight face . Structurally it is all over the place , the writing often derivative and the filmmaking inexpert . The pace is plodding and for all the undoubted design talent involved in the production , its imagery never achieves true wonder . Nevertheless , a few days after watching it I ca n't help feeling affection for it . There 's a charm in its amateurishness . <p> The film is scripted by Simon Farnaby , one-time member of The Mighty Boosh and a pivotal creator of the Horrible Histories television series . Farnaby , who appears in a minor part in the new film , had success in 2017 with Paddington 2 . Like that film , The Magic Faraway Tree combines an adult 's nostalgic fondness for the original source material with a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> A pivotal difference between this new film and Paddington 2 is that the adult characters are foregrounded . Claire Foy and Andrew Garfield play Polly and Tim Thompson . The film opens with Polly , a product designer , announcing that she has quit her job : the tension between her youthful creative hopes and the reality of being a corporate functionary has become too onerous . Tim , who is a stay-at-home dad , takes her resignation as inspiration . He brings out a dream book they compiled together as a young couple and , flicking through it , they settle on a cherished but long abandoned aspiration . They will commit to a rural retreat , she to become an artist and he to create a small business built on his homemade tomato sauce . <p> Not surprisingly , their three digital age children do n't take kindly to this . The oldest , Beth ( Delilah Bennett-Cardy ) , is on the cusp of adolescence and does n't want to leave behind the city and her friends , while Joe ( Phoenix Laroche ) worries @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Billie Gadsdon ) , shy and uncommunicative , shows a glimmer of interest in the move . <p> On the way to the small shack that is their new home , Fran encounters a sprite on the road . This woodland elf , Silky ( Nicola Coughlan ) , will be the conduit through which first Fran then all the Thompson children will discover the magic of the Faraway Tree , hidden deep in the enchanted wood at the edge of their new home . <p> It 's understandable that Farnaby and his director , Ben Gregor , wanted to update the story -- the parents in Blyton 's original stories are shadowy presences . However , the earnest anxiety with which the screenplay treats the children 's screen addictions feels forced . Equally artificial is the writing of the parents . Polly and Tim so dominate the first act that it undermines the film 's attempt at enchantment . The comedy of an urban family navigating the realities of living in a shambolic barn without running water and electricity falls flat . The writing is too crude , the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lazily paced . <p> The filmmakers have forgotten that as children , safety is a greater reward , more earnt , when we have the thrill of peril first . <p> Once Fran discovers the Faraway Tree and the magical folk who inhabit it , the story gains more energy . One of the pleasures of the original stories is in the admixture of feyness and stolidness that define the tree 's inhabitants . As a child reader , I adored the bourgeois archness of Moonface , played here by Nonso Anozie , and the absurdity of Saucepan Man ( Dustin Demri-Burns ) . There was a sly comedy in the neurotic obsession with cleanliness that defined Dame Washalot ( Jessica Gunning ) . Even the wraith , Silky , had an earthbound practicality . <p> It is a strength of the film that the actors playing these fairy creatures remain true to Blyton 's original conception . This domestication of the ethereal has been one of the most consistent criticisms of Blyton 's writing . We never felt threatened by the Faraway Tree 's residents , never felt the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , say , to J. ? M. Barrie 's Neverland . Blyton 's worlds never allowed the impingement of the surreal and the terrifying that is integral to the works of Lewis Carroll . <p> Re-reading the Faraway Tree books , one is struck by the simplicity and matter-of-factness of Blyton 's writing . For a young reader just starting on their journey into literature , there is joy in that safety . Anozie , Coughlan , Demri-Burns and Gunning are a wonderful quartet , their performances playfully eccentric yet never overwhelming . We understand why young Fran 's affection for these woodland creatures is immediate . <p> There was one unsettling threat in the Faraway Tree stories : the ever-changing lands that would appear atop the tree . I think the filmmakers have made a great mistake in not acknowledging that children take pleasure in being frightened . Fran 's first adventure is in the Land of Sweets and that episode is as saccharine as it sounds , as it was in the original story . Yet even when the children visit the Land of Wishes and things go @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the Land of Dame Snap , the set-ups are devoid of scariness , of dread . <p> The whole sequence in the Land of Dame Snap is dreadful . In Blyton 's original story , she was named Dame Slap , the headmistress of a tyrannical college where she administered smacks to any unruly children . More recent editions of the book have resulted in the name change , and now Dame Snap ( Rebecca Ferguson ) is just a nasty scold . As the children feel no fear at her harangues , the scenes are duds . We watch them in bored anticipation of the eventual escape . <p> The wretchedness of the Dame Snap episode underlines a failure of imagination in the conception and writing of the film . Farnaby and Gregor 's contemporary revising makes sense , but I think they have been timorous in their attempts to renew the tales . As a child I remember shivering in delicious fear when the children entered the Land of Topsy-Turvy . As the weight of what it would mean to live a life upside-down took hold , I @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ would take them back to the Faraway Tree . The filmmakers have forgotten that as children , safety is a greater reward , more earnt , when we have the thrill of peril first . Also , in fantasy , they can safely learn to negotiate danger . <p> It is a boon that the filmmakers secured Foy and Garfield to play the parents . These two formidable actors never condescend to the material . Their performances combine the exact right blend of light-heartedness and imagination so that we believe them as loving parents and a loving couple . The three children also give terrific performances . Their pragmatism is absolutely fitting for Blyton . <p> The morning after I watched the film , I flicked through some of my old copies of Blyton 's stories . I was struck by how much the Magic Faraway Tree books were written for very young readers . I am of a generation where Blyton 's books were a key introduction to the joys of reading , I devoured them again and again . Yet , it does n't take long to outgrow @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the attraction , soon become tedious . <p> I spent an hour of that morning immersed in Blyton 's first book about a young girl who is off to boarding school , to Malory Towers . Blyton was at her best in these school stories . Undoubtedly they too are compromised by her unreflective conservatism , full of moral homilies that seemed outdated even when I read them as a boy , yet the writing and tone are never patronising . She was capable of inventing fully realised adolescent characters . There are whole generations of queers , for example , who remain grateful for her character George in The Famous Five . <p> The adaptation of The Magic Faraway Tree wants to take us by the hand and make clear how much we have moved on from the world of middle-class mid 20th century Britain . Even as a young reader in the 1970s , I was already aware of how much had changed in the world from the one that Blyton was depicting . This is one of the problems with adults second-guessing what children think . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Tree is that its intended viewers are more inquisitive , more knowing , than the filmmakers think they are . This is a children 's film that needed less caution and much more magic . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on March 25 , 2026 as " Realms without peril " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . This is being fuelled by the growth in artificial intelligence and allowed to spread freely on social media , according to the findings of a Senate inquiry . <p> This misinformation presents a threat to action on climate change , but also challenges the health of Australia 's democracy , the committee found . AI was even used to generate fake content in some of the submissions to the inquiry . <p> Drawing on 247 written submissions and 11 days of public hearings -- including some extraordinary revelations I 'll get to shortly -- senators from all sides of politics heard about the challenge our society faces to combat misinformation and disinformation . <h> Why does misinformation matter ? <p> First , it 's important to understand why misinformation matters @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it . <p> Misinformation is the spread of false information , regardless of whether there is an intent to harm or mislead . But when an individual or organisation spreads misinformation with the intent to influence public opinion , this is known as disinformation . <p> Both are important . In democratic societies , public opinion is the link between what people want , their electoral behaviour , and what politicians do on their behalf . Democratic representation is therefore predicated on knowing and understanding public opinion . <p> If misinformation starts to warp or sever this link , our democratic societies can unravel . We only have to look across the Pacific to the United States to see what this looks like in real time . <h> What is happening in Australia ? <p> The inquiry uncovered countless instances where misinformation -- and often disinformation -- was affecting public opinion on everything , from wind farms and whales to electric vehicles and batteries . <p> Indeed , one of the motivations for the Senate inquiry was evidence that emerged in 2025 highlighting how anti-offshore wind campaigns had spread misinformation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the sunrise -- neither of which is true . <p> It is not only wind farms that have been the target . Misinformation about batteries is rife too . For example , testimony from a NSW farmer told how a 500 kilowatt-hour community battery in Narrabri , initially supported by the local council , was later blocked following a campaign driven by misinformation on Facebook . These pages claimed the battery would blow up , catch fire , and might even shut down the town -- assertions that were not supported by evidence . <p> For many people , misinformation and disinformation have become part of daily life . Survivors of the 2019 Black Summer bushfires submitted evidence describing how misinformation had created rifts in local NSW communities and driven family members apart . Those advocating for action on climate change had faced a torrent of abuse on social media , as lies about the causes of the fires spread online . <h> Who is funding and spreading it ? <p> In my own testimony before the committee , I described how research from more than 100 scholars around the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ influence the public , media and political arenas to slow , stop or reverse effective climate action . This is what we refer to as climate obstruction . <p> In Australia this is not just gas and coal companies . But there are other players too , such as trade associations , think tanks and PR firms , among many others , that have a history of opposing climate policies . <p> For example , Australians for Natural Gas , which appears to be a grassroots organisation that supports pro-gas policies , was in fact set up by the chief executive of gas company Tamboran Resources , with help from PR firm Freshwater Strategy , according to an investigation by the ABC . <p> My own research has shown industry lobby groups historically opposed to climate policies in the US spent US$3.4 billion ( A$4.88 billion ) on political activities , especially public relations , between 2008 and 2018 . In Australia , our knowledge of who is funding disinformation is hampered by a lack of transparency . <p> A number of participants to the Senate inquiry refused to reveal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ AI and social media <p> The committee 's report makes it clear that social media and AI are fuelling misinformation . Senators heard how the algorithms on social media platforms like Facebook , Instagram and TikTok often prioritised engagement over accuracy , " creating echo chambers that reinforce existing beliefs and can amplify misleading content " . <p> What is worse is that social media corporations are doing little to address it . Under a grilling from senators , Meta , which owns Facebook and Instagram , conceded it spends more on lobbying than fact-checking in Australia . <p> AI was also used to generate fake content in Senate submissions to the very inquiry investigating misinformation . It was uncovered that Rainforest Reserves Australia ( RRA ) , a conservative campaign group opposing renewable energy , had included information about wind farms that do not exist . It also cited academic articles that do not exist . <p> In one of the more ridiculous moments , when RRA was confronted by the media about its AI-influenced submissions , it sent a 1,500-word response . Later , it acknowledged this had @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ca n't make this stuff up ! <p> AI is also making it easier for groups to spread false information by generating fake social media posts , pictures and videos . <h> Combating climate misinformation <p> While the committee acknowledged " there is no simple fix for the spread of false and misleading information " , it recommended a series of important actions . These included : <p> Additional comments from senators went further . These included banning donations from fossil fuel industries and legislating truth in political advertising . Significantly , they also called for powers to compel social media companies to remove fake content and bots used in coordinated campaigns to obstruct climate action . <p> The federal government should act on these worthy recommendations before the next election . Otherwise , this problem will only grow . As the senators pointed out , nothing less than the health of our democracy is at stake . <p> When you login first time using a Social Login button , we collect your account public profile information shared by Social Login provider , based on your privacy settings . By Sam Roggeveen . <h> How the Iran war compels a rethink of US alliance <p> Let 's start by acknowledging that we do n't know how much worse the war with Iran could get . @@135763897 <h> Nyadol Nyuon NACC and the corruption of promise <p> You do not face a crisis of democracy unless the ordinary mechanism of democratic accountability has failed . The National Anti-Corruption Commission ( NACC ) was the body established to ensure this accountability existed in a system that appeared ever more unaccountable . Its establishment fulfilled a major election promise , made ahead of the Albanese government 's first term . <p> In early March , the commission delivered its first significant findings related to six individuals referred to it by the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme . The findings were published in a report that deputy commissioner Kylie Kilgour , who led the investigation team , said provided transparency as to how the conclusions about six individuals were reached . <p> Trust is a key principle of accountability . An application of the " trust principle " can be located within the history of anti-corruption oversight in Australia . In a Western Australian royal commission conducted more than 30 years ago , the inquiry into the corrupt political activities known as WA Inc. , the trust principle was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and agencies of government exist for the public , to serve the interests of the public " . <p> The trust principle is an architectural principle of democratic institutions , which flows from the nature of the democratic relationship between the representative and the represented . The notion that public power is held in trust for the public good is not a radical position . It is basic . Yet it is difficult to reconcile the trust principle with the findings of the NACC . <p> The commission found Scott Morrison had not engaged in corrupt conduct because , within the meaning of the National Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2022 , he did not act dishonestly . The report formed this view because it could not be proved that he knew or intended to proceed with the scheme in the face of a known legal obstacle . <p> That finding rested on two things . The first reason was the allegation that Morrison had expressed a desire to proceed without legislative amendment could not be established . The second reason was the assumption that , had Morrison suspected a problem , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ known that silence was the more dangerous option for him and his government . On the basis of this , his failure to act was proof he simply did not know . " Rather than being a reason to suspect a dishonest failure to inquire , " the report says , " the fact that Mr Morrison did not make further inquiries appears more probably consistent with him not having perceived there was a need to do so . " <p> Both positions are troubling in their own ways . <p> The finding that Morrison had not expressly said he wished to proceed was not only used to negate dishonest intent , it was also used to remove the foundation for any claim he had applied pressure on public servants that might have caused or contributed to their conduct to act dishonestly in finding a way to make the scheme work , regardless of its legality . <p> If the commission 's implicit premise is that communication is verbal , and as such pressure only exists when it is spoken , it has made two errors simultaneously . It has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about how power communicates . On the personal level , everyone has experienced communication that carried no words . Everyone has been in a meeting , a relationship , a workplace , where what was understood by everyone in the room was never said by anyone in the room . On the question of power , real power rarely speaks . It does not need to . The characteristic of power is in fact its ability to silence . <p> The commission 's inability to hear what was never said is not an evidentiary limitation . It is a failure to understand how power operates , a failure the law , in other contexts , has long since corrected . In employment law , the concept of constructive dismissal is the legal system 's own recognition that context communicates . An employer who never says " resign or be fired " can nonetheless have communicated exactly that through the structure of the working environment . The law built a doctrine around this recognition . <p> In the end , the commission found that a former prime minister did not act @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ... It appears ignorance of the law is no excuse for an average citizen , but ignorance of the obligations of your public offices is sufficient excuse for a politician . <p> We must seriously wonder whether a National Anti-Corruption Commission that makes this finding is set to see the most common and consequential form of communication that its mandate requires it to detect , assess and prevent . <p> A counterargument is available to the critique above . It could be said this critique , however accurate as a matter of institutional design , asks the commission to exceed its statutory mandate . This argument is that the Act is built around dishonesty as a legal concept with a subjective mental element , and that the commission was constrained not by naivety but by law . That objection , however , brings us back to the trust principle . <p> The commission 's second finding was that , had Morrison known or suspected there was a legal problem , he would have acted on that knowledge , because " as a member of parliament and minister of many years @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ were he to do so , there would be a high chance of the deception soon being discovered and of his and his government 's subjection to the inevitably adverse political consequences that would follow " . <p> His failure to act was therefore read not as a choice but as proof that there was nothing on which to act . The reasoning is circular : he would have acted if he knew ; he did not act ; therefore he did not know . <p> The defining failure of circular reasoning is that nothing is actually grounded because it assumes rather than proves . In the commission 's case , the premise that Morrison would have acted if he knew is itself unproved . It is an assumption about how a rational political actor behaves . The conclusion that he did not know is derived entirely from that assumption . <p> The commission is essentially using an assumed behavioural theory to establish a finding of fact about Morrison 's state of mind . That is a significant logical step . It also reverses the expectation of the trust principle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and replaces it with political rationality based on the logic of self-preservation or the preservation of one 's political party . <p> On the commission 's finding , a minister is exonerated not because he served the public faithfully but because a self-interested politician would have acted differently . The standard by which he is measured is not what the people he governed were entitled to expect of him but what his own career required of him . <p> This is a reorientation of the very foundation on which ministerial accountability rests . It is a fundamental shift from obligation to the public to obligation to oneself . It is possible , maybe even reasonable , to argue this is not what the commission 's reasoning supports . It would be fair to point out , as outlined in the commission 's report , it acknowledged that public officers stand in a fiduciary relationship to the people and owe them an inescapable obligation of the highest fidelity . <p> All of that , however , only points to what the commission said and not what it actually did . Morrison @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ against his self-interest . By stating its own standard and then departing from it , the commission treated the substantive issue as decorative . <p> There is another question , besides the question the commission appeared to have asked , which is why in the first place was Morrison 's rational self-interest as a politician even a relevant consideration in an analysis founded on a fiduciary relationship ? <p> There is a distinction between the politician as an individual and the politician as the holder of a public office . This is a distinction with significance in itself , as well as having historic backing , in the context of Australia 's anti-corruption oversights . It is questionable that Morrison 's political self-preservation is a relevant consideration to the question of whether public power was exercised as the fiduciary relationship requires . In fact , it may be exactly the kind of private calculation that the accountability standard exists to exclude . <p> That was precisely what Western Australia 's Royal Commission into Commercial Activities of Government highlighted as concerning in 1992 . In the context of investigating corruption and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ministers had elevated personal or party advantage over their constitutional obligation to act in the public interest . " <p> While the NACC and the WA royal commission may not share the same legislative framework , they do share the foundational principle that public power is held in trust for the public benefit . For both findings to be true , the trust principle would have to have ceased to be the architectural principle of democratic institutions between 1992 and 2026 . <p> It is impossible to simultaneously hold that elevating personal advantage over constitutional obligation is the conduct accountability must address , and that a minister 's political self-interest is the measure by which their conduct is exonerated . The commission 's position does not appear to suggest that the democratic legal order has evolved in this manner . It still acknowledges that public officers stand in a fiduciary relationship to the people and owe them an inescapable obligation of the highest fidelity . <p> In the final analysis , it is difficult to understand what useful insight the commission 's first significant finding has delivered . To find @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ new . It is , precisely , the complaint . The public is not unaware of this . That is not what concerns them . @@135763900 <h> Stan Grant Pauline Hanson and the end of nationhood <p> So , Peter Malinauskas wants us all to have a cup of tea or a frothy and talk footy . Better still , he says , if we read some Henry Lawson . This is the re-elected South Australian Labor premier 's banal appeal for unity in a bitterly divided world . <p> Malinauskas is trying to head off the potent patriotic lure of Pauline Hanson 's One Nation , which attracted a higher primary vote in South Australia than the Liberals . Good luck with that . <p> Malinauskas has won a landslide victory , but a closer look reveals Labor 's primary vote is lower than at the last state election in 2022 . The political and cultural winds are in Hanson 's sails . <p> The former fish and chip shop owner has been to jail and had her conviction quashed . She has danced on television and survived 30 years in the public eye . Despite -- or because of -- her odious political stunts , her vilification of racial and religious groups , Pauline would not be short of supporters with whom to share a frothy . What Malinauskas and Hanson are hitting on is the profound need for roots in a rootless world . <p> Who are we ? What does it mean to belong ? Who decides ? These questions are a faultline running through Western liberal democracies . They have powered the resurgence of the political right in Europe , inspired the Brexit vote in Great Britain and seen the rise of Nigel Farage 's Reform UK movement . They have put Donald Trump in the White House . <p> Authoritarian leaders play the identity card , too . Russia 's Vladimir Putin and China 's Xi Jinping appeal to toxic resentment and myths of national glory , while India 's Narendra Modi successfully peddles his version of Hindu nationalism and sectarian division . <p> Australia has done nation building better @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ but arch political populism has now found its way here and it will gain even more momentum . Inflation , immigration and culture wars will supercharge Hansonism . Opponents make a big mistake mocking or underestimating Hanson . They always have . <p> Populists like Hanson are devastatingly effective at tribal warfare . Her followers want to take us back to the future . It is an irrational response to an irrational world . It is also political dynamite . <p> There is a reckoning in Australia . <p> As elsewhere , it will be nasty . It will be unpredictable . It is also long overdue . The world has been here many times before and history tells us it has led to bloodshed and revolution . A frothy and some laconic Aussie poetry will not calm this identity war . <p> In 1882 , French thinker Ernest Renan asked : What is a nation ? His essay is worth returning to . Nations then were new . The world had seen civilisations , states and empires , but nations as we know them are modern . <p> Renan @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ called nations a " soul , a spiritual principle " . Nations , he wrote , are forged on two principles : " One is the possession in common of a rich legacy of memories ; the other is present-day consent , the desire to live together . " <p> The nation , he wrote , is a daily plebiscite . Nations share an undivided heritage . Like the individual , he said , a nation " is the culmination of a long past of endeavours , sacrifice and devotion " . <p> Nations are built on memories , but Renan , with the memory of his own nation 's bloody revolution , said nations are also built on forgetting . History , he said , constitutes a danger for the principle of nationality . " Indeed , historical enquiry brings to light deeds of violence which took place at the origin of all political formations ... " <p> I would agree . Too much history suffocates a nation . Above all , Renan said , nations must not be things of blood and soil and God . He wrote @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nor his language , nor of his religion , nor of the course of rivers nor of the direction taken by mountain chains . A large aggregate of men , healthy in mind and warm of heart , creates the kind of moral conscience which we call a nation . " <p> Critics say Renan failed his own test . He is accused of Eurocentrism , Gallic nationalism , republican racism . That criticism may underline that all nations are paradoxical and hypocritical . <p> Yet Renan 's essay resonates powerfully today . What are we prepared to forget ? Can we tame the tribalism of blood and soil ? How do we build a shared heritage on increasingly irreconcilable difference ? <p> If anything , the stakes are higher today . Globalism has shaken the foundations of the nation state . Nationality and allegiance is fluid . Trade and culture is unbounded . The global movement of people is testing the limits of cohesion , tolerance , respect and forbearance in ways Renan could not have seen . <p> He saw America as the birthplace of modern nationalism . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shared sense of purpose or belonging . <p> Nations were simply too big and diverse for everyone to know each other , so they required a shared imagination . Nations , he said , were sovereign and limited . They were the equivalent of secular religions : a larger social and historical context that transcends individuals . <p> In the 21st century , the question of the nation is up for grabs again . For one thing , we do not forget . Historical grievance is a cancer on the body politic . We are not imagined communities ; we are fractured , suspicious and often hostile communities . <p> Our political discourse is shrill , ungracious and embittered , a terrible foundation for belonging . As American political scientist Mark Lilla laments , there is no shared " we " . Islamophobia , racism and xenophobia are irremovable stains on our polity . The scourge of anti-Semitism is resurgent globally and has devastated our own nation in ways we have not even begun to reconcile . <p> Foreign wars are now played out on our streets . Australians are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australia was once a nation where old enmities were largely buried , now they are rallying cries . Peter Malinauskas urges us to talk more about footy than faith . He misses the point . We probably already do , but faith shouts louder . <p> Since the Al Qaeda attacks on the United States on September 11 , 2001 , Islamist terrorism has presented an existential threat for the world . America and allies have fought poorly conceived and poorly executed wars on multiple fronts , upending nations and casting unprecedented numbers of people adrift , which has put enormous stress on social cohesion . <p> Nations are unmoored . @@135763902 <h> Booker Prize-winner David Szalay , in Australia for the Melbourne and Sydney writers ' festivals , has written the dissociations of his peripatetic life into a series of novels . By James Bradley . <h> Author David Szalay on writing the Booker Prize-winning Flesh <p> Some Booker Prize winners feel both thrilling and inevitable . David Szalay 's Flesh is one of them . One of the most striking novels of recent years , it traces the life of a young Hungarian man from his teens to his 40s and from Hungary to England and back . Written in a radically stripped back and deliberately affectless prose , it offers a deeply moving portrait of a kind of man not often glimpsed in fiction . It also goes beyond that , to craft a fascinating and unsettling portrait of the rootlessness and often-invisible violence that shapes contemporary society . <p> Szalay ( pronounced " SOL-loy " ) , who is visiting Australia for the Melbourne ( May 7-10 ) and Sydney ( May 17-24 ) writers ' festivals , began Flesh in Hungary , where he had been living @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ chapter in a life shaped by movement and migration . <p> Born to a Canadian mother and a Hungarian -- Canadian father in 1974 , his parents moved first to Beirut and then to London when he was only one year old . In his 30s , he left London , going first to Brussels and then to Hungary , where he met his German-born wife . More recently he and his wife moved again , this time to Vienna . While it was n't the main factor in their decision , neither he nor his wife " were very comfortable with the dominant political tone in Hungary " . <p> Szalay says moving around in this way has given him " a particular perspective " that has been " very important in terms of my sense of who I am and in terms of my books " . This feeling of displacement is central to Flesh . " When I started the novel , I 'd been living already in Hungary for quite a few years , but I did n't feel entirely at home there , and not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ well , I never will , " he says . " But at the same time , I 'd become a bit distanced from England and from London and was n't 100 per cent in tune with those places either ... it felt like I was stretched or somehow stuck between the two places , and I wanted to write a book that used that feeling somehow . " <p> Istv ? n , the young Hungarian man at the centre of the novel , is a remarkable creation . The first time we encounter him he is 15 . Already oddly untethered , he is told by his mother to help the 40-something woman who lives in a neighbouring flat with her shopping . Before long Istv ? n and the woman are sleeping together . <p> Because we experience the relationship from Istv ? n 's perspective , the novel allows us to see how Istv ? n is manipulated and groomed by his neighbour and the degree to which this trauma leaves him profoundly unfixed in himself . The relationship leads to the first of the book @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forward , finding Istv ? n following a period in a juvenile offenders ' home , then recently returned from a tour in Iraq , then moving on to England , where he becomes a security guard assigned to protect a super-rich couple . After an affair with his employer 's wife , Helen , he joins the world of the 1 per cent and attempts to establish himself among London 's elite . <p> " When I wrote the first chapter I very consciously decided that the emotional impact could be maximised by not stating or describing emotions directly . " <p> In the immediate aftermath of its Booker win , much of the commentary about Flesh sought to frame Istv ? n as an avatar of contemporary masculinity and its various crises . Chair of the judging panel Roddy Doyle said the novel " homes in on a working-class man , which ordinarily does n't get much of a look-in " , presenting " us with a certain type of man " and " invites us to look behind the face " . Similarly , The Times bestowed @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " upon it and observed that it " seems likely to appeal to that elusive creature , the 21st-century male reader of novels " . <p> Szalay both recognises and resists these sorts of readings of Flesh . On the one hand he admits he knew " the book would be to some extent read and received in terms of contemporary masculinity and questions around it " but he also did n't want that to overwhelm it . <p> " Certainly that was n't the dominant thing for me when I was writing it , " he says . " Istv ? n 's far too complex a character ultimately to be taken as only that . And the book has wider interests and wider concerns . " He acknowledges , though , that the book is " also inescapably about that , and that 's fine " . <p> This ambiguity is of a piece with the novel 's general elusiveness . Despite filling the frame , Istv ? n remains a curiously unknowable presence , a character defined as much by the gaps and omissions in our understanding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ never learn his family name , nor anything much about his upbringing . His father is simply absent without explanation . His mother remains nameless . Although we know he is from Hungary , and in the opening line are informed that " when he 's fifteen he and his mother move to a new town and he starts at a new school " , we never learn which town he came from or where this new town is . Even his apparently imposing physicality remains essentially undefined . <p> The novel 's structure contributes to this sense of absence . Earlier books of Szalay 's such as 2016 's Booker-shortlisted All That Man Is and 2018 's Turbulence are structured as discontinuous narratives that leap between characters and places . In Turbulence each of the fragments focuses on a passenger in an airplane , who connects to the next in one way or another . In All That Man Is , which leaps between the lives of nine different men separated by geography and personal history -- beginning with a 17-year-old student and ending with a 73-year-old confronting the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ even more tenuous , and despite a few scattered narrative links are mostly thematic . Indeed the sections are so disparate that some early reviews of All That Man Is treated the book as linked short stories rather than a fully fledged novel . <p> With its focus on a single character , there is no question Flesh is a novel . Yet the long gaps between the sections leave many questions unanswered and contribute to the remarkable combination of intense intimacy and distanced unknowability , the sense that while we observe Istv ? n very closely he remains somehow opaque , even to himself . <p> This effect is heightened further by how the novel privileges surfaces and appearances , effectively rejecting the conventional literary preoccupation with interiority . In its place it offers a deliberately denuded prose from which every rough surface has been planed away . Conversations are flat , almost affectless , often reduced to sequences of repetition and restatement . <p> Szalay says the technique grew out of his work on Turbulence , which began life as a series of short stories written for the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 15-minute radio slot , there was a very hard limit on the number of words and it meant I had to think very carefully always about exactly what to include , because each story was only a couple of thousand words , " he tells me . " That got me into this habit of writing with a ruthless concision that was focused on what was essential to the story and to the situation I was describing . I like that style because it feels effective and I enjoyed working like that and it sort of carried over . So there 's no doubt that Flesh has a more pared-down and concise style than any of my previous novels . " <p> As a literary device this is both destabilising and provocative : following its Booker win Roddy Doyle reflected , " I do n't think I 've read a novel that uses the white space on the page so well . It 's as if the author ... is inviting the reader to fill the space , to observe -- almost to create -- the character with him . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Every word matters ; the spaces between the words matter . " <p> Szalay agrees . " When I wrote the first chapter I very consciously decided that the emotional impact could be maximised by not stating or describing emotions directly but by making them implicit and leaving the reader to supply the emotion themselves . I think the whole book works like that at its moments of greatest emotional impact . " <p> He concedes the decision to leave out so much was n't without its risks : " I was n't quite sure how people were going to react to either the character of Istv ? n , who does n't explain himself , or to the narrative voice of the book , which does n't explain him to the reader in any direct way .
