As its title suggests , Flesh is very much a book @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world . " I wanted to write a book about , in a way , life as a physical experience , or at least that took the physicality of life as its starting point , " says Szalay . But Istv ? n 's disconnection is also at least partly the result of his abuse at the hands of his neighbour , which shapes and suffuses his life . <p> Szalay says while he 's sceptical of " the ability of talking things out to remove burdens ... the whole book in a way could be seen as a processing of those events " . " The trajectory of his life is set by that , " he says . " But also , inevitably , the trajectory of who he is . " Szalay points to the way the events of the first chapter are reflected over and over again across Istv ? n 's life . " There are echoes of it throughout the book . Obviously , his relationship with Helen in London begins with a weirdly eerily similar power dynamic . " Likewise , " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ recurs several times throughout the book , and obviously towards the end in a very , very significant way " . <p> Simultaneously , the book 's blankly affectless prose captures something essential about the social and psychic landscape of the world it inhabits . In Flesh it goes deeper . In his book Filterworld , the American writer Kyle Chayka writes about the " algorithmic aesthetic " he dubs " Airspace " : the " strangely frictionless geography " that characterises the weird homogeneity of contemporary cafes , airports , workspaces and more . An expression of the deadening alienation of capitalism 's fantasy of frictionlessness , the algorithmic aesthetic strips away " self and surroundings until everything becomes smooth and uniform " . <p> The denuded prose of Flesh powerfully captures this sense of numbness and exhaustion , its elision of deeper human meaning . Speaking about one of the book 's most important @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's wife , Helen -- Szalay notes that despite her and the business of her career playing an important role in the book 's narrative , he made a point of never describing her art . " We do n't learn anything about the actual art , because that 's not important , " he says . " From the perspective of the book the art is just a social signifier and a commodity . @@135763905 <h> Mark Oppenheimer Judy Blume : A Life <p> When I was 11 , I set myself the challenge of reading every book I had not yet borrowed in our school library . My favourite genres were fantasy and historical fiction , so the shelf devoted to the contemporary realist books of Judy Blume was my toughest test . @@135763906 <h> Venison schnitzel with kimchi coleslaw <p> Jo Barrett is a chef , co-founder of Wildpie and the author of Sustain . She is a food editor of The Saturday Paper . <p> Credit : Photographed remotely by Earl Carter <p> Despite being one of the most nutrient-dense proteins on the planet , venison remains a fringe meat in Australia . It 's overshadowed by beef , lamb , pork and chicken . It is high in protein , iron and B vitamins and naturally low in fat . From a nutritional and environmental perspective , it is hard to argue against . Given the abundance of deer , it 's surprising venison is n't more readily available or more commonly cooked in Australian homes . <p> There are reasons for this . Until recently , venison has been difficult to find . For some , a first encounter with poorly handled or overcooked game has been enough to put them off entirely . ( I remember my first , cold , undercooked , gamy tenderloin ) . For many others , the barrier is simply a lack of knowledge @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it is n't as widely accepted as it is in New Zealand , Europe or the United States . I was once firmly in that camp myself but now call myself a hunter . <p> Australia is now home to six established species of introduced deer : fallow , rusa , red , chital , hog and sambar . Fallow deer are smaller , mild-flavoured and tender ; sambar are larger and also have a mild flavour ; red deer sit somewhere in between in size , with a more distinct flavour , as do rusa deer . Chital tend to be finer-grained and slightly sweeter . Hog deer are smaller , delicate , though far less common and the only deer that 's protected . They require a tag to be hunted . <p> These differences are shaped not only by species but by environment , diet and movement , much like the differences we accept and embrace with beef and lamb . <p> In Victoria alone , there are estimated to be more than one million wild deer . Populations are managed through government culling programs to protect @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to prevent road accidents . In most cases , animals are killed and not recovered , as the primary objective is population control not harvesting . It represents a significant amount of wasted , edible protein . Learning about this was what first sparked my interest in cooking with wild , invasive species . <p> One common concern with the consumption of wild venison is that parasites may be present , but all meat sold for human consumption is processed through licensed facilities and checked by registered meat inspectors , so it is safe to eat . The meat also should always be properly cooked . <p> The beauty of this venison schnitzel is its accessibility . It does n't rely on a specific cut ; backstrap , rump , top side or loin all work and the technique delivers tenderness and flavour . Also , who does n't love a schnitzel ? Paired with a sharp , crunchy kimchi coleslaw , one ingredient expressed through different textures , it 's a familiar , approachable way to bring venison off the sideline and onto the everyday table . <p> Ingredients @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Serves 2 <p> 2 x 200g venison steaks ( topside , rump , back strap or tenderloin ) <p> ? cup plain flour <p> salt and pepper <p> 1 egg <p> 1 tbsp milk <p> ? cup panko breadcrumbs <p> 4 tbsp ghee <p> ? cabbage <p> ? cup kimchi <p> 2 spring onions <p> 1 tbsp kimchi juice <p> 2 tbsp sour cream <p> 2 tbsp mayonnaise ( I use Kewpie ) <p> 1 lemon ( cut two wedges and juice the rest ) <p> Method <p> Place the venison steaks between two pieces of baking paper . Use a rolling pin or a meat tenderiser to evenly bash the steaks flat until they are one centimetre thick . <p> Season the flour with salt and pepper and spread it onto a plate . <p> Whisk the egg and milk together until homogenised . <p> Spread the panko breadcrumbs onto a plate . <p> Coat each steak in flour , tap away the excess and then dip the dusted venison into the egg mixture . Once completely coated , remove and press into the breadcrumbs , making sure @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the ghee in a large pan over a medium heat . Drop a few crumbs into the ghee ; once they bubble , it 's hot enough to add the schnitzel . <p> Cook for two to three minutes on each side until they are golden brown . <p> Remove from the pan and place onto paper towel or a cake rack . Season with salt . <p> Thinly slice the cabbage , kimchi and spring onions and place into a medium-sized bowl . <p> Add the dressing to the cabbage and mix until evenly coated . Season to taste with salt , and a little more kimchi juice if you like the salad more tangy . <p> Serve each schnitzel with some coleslaw and a lemon wedge . <p> This article was first published in the print edition of The Saturday Paper on March 28 , 2026 as " On the wild side " . <p> For almost a decade , The Saturday Paper has published Australia 's leading writers and thinkers . @@135790712 <p> Last year , historian Adam Tooze wrote about the tendency to describe the history of energy as a " series of transitions " . In this story , wood gave way to coal , coal to gas , and now fossil fuels are being replaced by renewables . This allows us to believe in history as a tale of progress . In turn , it is that story of progress which allows us to believe that whatever we are now living through , however troubling it might seem , is a necessary step -- because soon we will arrive at a better destination . <p> The problem is that these " transitions " never actually happen . ( Tooze is drawing on the work of historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz ) . The history of energy use is that energy sources are never actually replaced . Instead , they are added to each other . In fact , Tooze writes , the world now uses more wood than it has at any point in its past -- and the same goes for coal . <p> Illustration by Joe Benke <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ better about our own time -- is false . Suddenly , Australia 's current policy of continuing to export fossil fuels reads differently : not as a stop on the way to somewhere better but as yet another step on the way to somewhere worse . <p> All this came to mind as I was considering the fact that , a decade ago , this seemed like the era of climate doom . Around then , I attended a festival where novelist Junot Diaz spoke about the boom in dystopian fiction . Taking his cue from the Marxist cultural critic Fredric Jameson , he laid out the logic behind this boom . It had become easier for us to fast-forward to the end of the world than face the fact we were still at a point when the end of the world might be averted . That would require work : it would mean changing our lives . Far more convenient to begin to accept apocalypse . <p> Advertisement <p> Perhaps , before then , there was a more hopeful point at which we imagined we might address climate change @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , since then , we have simply added new problems . As everyone knows , this is the era of polycrisis . <h> Related Article <p> Various moods have been attributed to this era : anxiety , anger , confusion . By now , though , it is most accurate to talk in terms of fear . <p> In part , this is because the accumulation has hit a certain point : the other reactions no longer seem adequate . But it is also because fear is more specific than the others . Anxiety , anger and confusion can all be amorphous : their causes can be various and diffuse . Actual fear , though , is more specific , activated in relation to a particular threat . <p> Many have experienced climate anxiety . But fear ? Fear only enters the scene at certain times -- during the 2019 bushfires , say . It was not only the scale of the fires but the fact so many of us living in cities smelt them , saw the pall they cast . They became real to us -- and therefore @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fear arrived again , in the knowledge we might die . More recently , many felt financial fear as prices surged and any sense of control vanished . Today 's crazy petrol prices reactivate this . <h> Related Article <p> Then there are far more significant fears , felt by specific groups . Jewish people have lived in well-founded fear of both antisemitism and antisemitic violence . Many other groups , in particular Muslims , have felt increased fear as racism becomes less taboo . <p> And then there is fear of artificial intelligence -- growing among ordinary people and underestimated by Australian politicians . Again , these are not vague anxieties , but fears based on retrenchments in the thousands . <p> This week , senior members of the government will meet the head of AI company Anthropic . Dario Amodei has warned that half of all entry-level office jobs could go ; that there is a possible future in which " 20 per cent of people do n't have jobs " and inequality " becomes scary " . How much will this figure in discussions ? <p> Advertisement @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ dominate this moment . Junot Diaz was right : we have , as a species , continued to fail to take seriously our status as the final generations during which something meaningful might be done on climate . A similar failure to act applies to the rise of authoritarianism . Nobody found an answer to Donald Trump -- instead , America invited him back -- and his second term has been far worse than the first . <h> Related Article <p> This is the pattern that repeats : a failure to meaningfully deal with crisis , followed by the situation deteriorating . With good reason , we are losing faith in our ability to confront these crises . The pandemic was , at first glance , an exception . Australia did well ; we came out the other side . In the moment , it was managed ( albeit with some significant failings ) . But did we learn from it ? <p> Former Labor official Kos Samaras recently argued that Victoria is still suffering the political fallout ; that true acknowledgment of Victorians ' experiences was never made . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : " The clock of normal politics resumes ticking . But the people who lived through it do n't forget . They just have n't been given the language , or the space , to say what they know . " <p> We all learnt things about inequality and our failures as a society to value what matters . But our politicians act as though we still do n't know these things . <p> Advertisement <p> The very real fear that has spread through our society these past few years , then , has three parts . We are scared of actual events . We are frightened that they wo n't be dealt with -- not meaningfully -- because that has been our recent experience . And we are increasingly immune to reassurance because we are starting to realise that too many of the stories we have been told -- about progress and optimism and governments that have things in hand and our best interests at heart -- were only ever stories . <p> Sean Kelly is a regular columnist and a former adviser to prime ministers Julia Gillard and Kevin Rudd .

Far from it . <p> Over 11 days of hearings and hundreds of submissions , the inquiry assembled a substantial body of evidence pointing to a growing " information integrity gap " that is distorting public debate , delaying policy , undermining trust in science and institutions , and posing a real threat to Australian democracy . <p> The inquiry heard extensive evidence that misinformation and disinformation are not isolated incidents but systemic and increasingly sophisticated . <p> Experts warned that digital platforms are amplifying false and distorted claims through opaque algorithms , while the rapid rise of artificial intelligence is accelerating an explosion of deceptive content . <h> A strong diagnosis , but a cautious prescription <p> The inquiry 's main recommendations set out a broad , whole-of-government approach to improving " information integrity " across climate and energy . <p> They call for adopting international frameworks , boosting funding for regulators , research and media , improving transparency around political and corporate influence , strengthening digital literacy , and enhancing oversight of digital platforms @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> But largely high-level . <p> They sketch the architecture of a response , rather than the detailed blueprint needed to deliver it . <p> And that is the central tension of this report . <p> Because it 's emerge . <h> Dig deeper <p> A majority of the committee -- including Greens chair Peter Whish-Wilson , the two Labor senators , independent David Pocock and Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan -- used our information environment , " Pocock and McLachlan were blunt in their assessment : " The committee 's report stops short of recommending the structural reforms needed to address underlying problems . Farmers for Climate Action , for example , detailed the use of fake social media profiles impersonating real Australians to create the illusion of widespread opposition to renewable energy . <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ relies heavily on voluntary industry codes and lacks enforceable obligations , leaving a significant gap in the ability to deal with false and misleading content . <p> Nor is there a clear legal obligation for platforms to remove bot accounts or label automated content -- a gap that experts warned will become more dangerous as AI tools advance . <p> " This regulatory gap is indefensible , " write Pocock and McLachlan , who argue that legislation is needed to force platforms to detect and remove bots , and to provide transparency around the algorithms that shape public discourse . <p> " The algorithms on which they base their business models now determine what millions of Australians see , hear and read . @@135815881 <p> Two new level crossings powered entirely by solar and battery power have been unveiled in northern New South Wales , part of the Inland Rail freight rail link that is being built to connect Melbourne to Brisbane . <p> Billed as Australia 's largest freight rail infrastructure project , Inland Rail is a once-in-a-generation project connecting Melbourne and Brisbane via regional Victoria , New South Wales , and Queensland . <p> The 12 individual projects together will span over 1,600 kilometres , and once completed Inland Rail will provide a 24-hour transit time for freight travelling between the two cities . <p> The two solar-powered level crossings were unveiled as part of the finishing works on the Narrabri to North Star ( N2NS ) Phase 1 section of the project . <p> The two new level crossings -- one located north of Moree and the other north of Narrabri -- are the first solar-powered level crossings on Inland Rail as well as parent company 's Australian Rail Track Corporation ( ARTC ) , which operates and maintains Australia 's national rail network . <p> Image Credit : Inland Rail @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " passive " level crossings -- those with no boom gates and only a sign such as ' Stop ' or ' Give Way ' that require drivers to look for trains directly -- to active crossings powered by a fully solar-powered standalone power system ( SAPS ) . <p> The upgrade is a huge leap and a potential boon for the country 's rail network . Level crossings , complete with automated boom gate and flashing lights , traditionally rely on grid-connected electricity and a battery back-up system . <p> In metropolitan parts of Australia this is a simple process , but across regional and rural Australia , where there are often scarce or no electricity infrastructure , level crossings are prohibitively expensive and complicated to build . <p> By relying on a solar and battery SAPS , Inland Rail avoided the need to connect to any existing power infrastructure or build new electrical assets , therefore also reducing land access requirements and minimising the impact on adjacent landholders . <p> Both of the new solar-powered level crossings now feature high-intensity LED flashing lights , bells , and retro-reflective @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the level crossings will work overnight or as an emergency backup , while a communications system allows for remote monitoring and fault alarms . <p> The ARTC is also planning to deploy solar-powered signalling systems at other locations across the alignment to supply electricity once Inland Rail becomes operational . <p> " Utilising solar-powered standalone power systems avoids impacts to local communities , clearing and the environment and reduces the cost of Inland Rail , " said a spokesperson for Inland Rail . <p> Joshua S. @@135847675 <h> One-time NASA caravan weather station plays global role <p> Despite its tiny size , Cape Grim station in Tasmania has played a key role in world science . Photo : HANDOUT/CSIRO <p> In 1976 , a former NASA caravan containing scientific equipment was perched on the edge of a remote cliff . <p> Since then , Cape Grim station in Tasmania 's northwest has played a key role in world science including in the phase-out of ozone-depleting substances such as chlorofluorocarbons which were used extensively in the 20th century as refrigerants and aerosol propellants . <p> The station , currently a more robust structure with bunk beds and a kitchen , monitors the " world 's cleanest air " which travels across the Southern Ocean . <p> Cape Grim station is marking 50 years since it first started recording observations . ( PR IMAGE PHOTO ) <p> For 24 hours a day , air is drawn through inlets - one located 80m up a tower - and analysed in real time . <p> Samples are also put in tanks and stored at a CSIRO lab in Melbourne which has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ principal experimental scientist Paul Krummel is one of several scientists who 'll be at the station on Wednesday for the 50th anniversary of when measurements were first taken . <p> " There have been massive contributions to global science from this station . It 's one of the longest running stations in the world , " he said . <p> " It 's a magical place . Once you 've been here a few times , it grabs hold of you . " <p> Cape Grim air samples are stored at a CSIRO lab in Melbourne , archiving them for over four decades . ( PR IMAGE PHOTO ) <p> Data from the station has been used in all five Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reports and underpinned hundreds of research papers . <p> It has also monitored the quality of Melbourne 's air and helped detect illegal emissions in China . <p> CSIRO senior principal research scientist Melita Keywood is working on a project examining atmospheric aerosols , which influence how light and heat reach the earth 's surface . <p> Despite some challenges , the station 's location @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a baseline . <p> " It can be very windy , we 've seen some of our instruments get blown over , " Dr Keywood , who has been coming to Cape Grim for 20 years , said . <p> Scientists have described the Cape Grim station as a " magical place " . ( HANDOUT/CSIRO ) <p> The long-term data is critical for understanding changes in the atmosphere over time and how to manage them in the future , she said . <p> " We have seen an ongoing increase in CO2 over the last 50 years from human-induced activities , " she said . <p> " However , we have also seen a decrease in the pollutant black carbon and ozone-depleting substances like CFC-11 , showing us that international efforts to reduce pollution , like the Montreal Protocol , can be effective . "

@@135847923 <p> Australian solar innovator RayGen has successfully deployed its unique technology using concentrated solar power to produce and store both clean electricity and thermal energy in a first international project in Brazil . <p> Located at a demonstration site in Brazil operated by AXIA Energia , formerly known as Eletrobras , the 1-megawatt ( MW ) PV Ultra system consists of a heliostat field , receiver tower , PV Ultra modules , and plant control system . <p> In addition to being able to feed solar electricity directly to the grid , RayGen 's PV Ultra is also able to store energy as cold and hot water in two water pits . <p> The cold water pit is " charged " using electricity and a standard ammonia-cycle chiller , while the hot water is sourced from RayGen 's solar system or a heat pump . When electricity is required , the temperature difference between the two water pits drives an organic Rankine cycle ( ORC ) turbine . <p> Image Credit : RayGen , via LinkedIn <p> " This is a proud moment for RayGen and for Australian innovation and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " Our unique technology , which generates clean electricity and thermal energy , is being rolled out internationally . <p> " It has been a pleasure working with AXIA . @@135847927 <p> A group of researchers from Japan and Germany may have conjured up a " dream technology " that could one day supercharge solar energy conversion to levels around 130 per cent , compared with the sub-30 per cent levels we see today . <p> In a paper recently published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society , a research team led by Kyushu University in Japan , in collaboration with Johannes Gutenberg University ( JGU ) Mainz in Germany , demonstrated a technique capable of generating and harvesting more solar energy than ever before . <p> The team is hoping to overcome what was believed to be an impossible-to-break " physical ceiling " to solar conversion , the impenetrability for laypeople of the research itself is unsurprising . The premise of the research , however , has to do with the way in which solar power is generated . <p> Planet Earth is bombarded by enormous amounts of energy from the Sun -- a fact which clean energy proponents have long publicised . Solar energy has the potential , like wind energy , to provide virtually all of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ currently only capture a fraction of the amount of energy the Sun is pouring down on the planet . <p> The Kyushu University press release attempts to clarify the problem with an analogy , picturing a relay race among photons from sunlight that strike a semiconductor and pass their energy on to electrons , activating them and driving an electric current . <p> These photonic runners , however , " vary in ability " , and include lower-energy infrared photos that are unable to excite electrons , while higher-energy photos , like those in blue light , lose their excess as heat . " As a result , solar cells can use only about one-third of the sunlight , " a physical " ceiling " that is known as the Shockley -- Queisser limit and one that has long challenged scientists . <p> In order to break through this limit , scientists have " two main strategies " , according to Yoichi Sasaki , associate professor at Kyushu University 's Faculty of Engineering . " One is to convert lower-energy infrared photons into higher energy visible photons . The other @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fission ( SF ) to generate two excitons from a single exciton photon . " <p> Singlet fission is able to split a high-energy singlet exciton into two lower-energy spin-triplet excitons , a process which theoretically doubles the energy of the original photon . <p> This process has recently been at the forefront of solar research . Last year , singlet fission was described by one group of researchers from the University of NSW as providing a " scalable pathway to high efficiency silicon photovoltaics " . <p> But capturing singlet fission-born excitons has remained a challenge for researchers , even though some organic semiconductors like tetracene exhibit the process . <p> It is at this point that the researchers from Kyushu University and JGU Mainz turned to metal complexes -- molecules whose structures can be flexibly designed -- and found that a molybdenum-based " spin-flip " emitter serves as an ideal harvester of excitons after fission . <p> In these flexibly designed molecules , an electron 's spin is flipped during the absorption or emission of near-infrared light , enabling the system to accept the triplet energy produced in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the energy levels , were able to suppress the wasteful FRET process and allow the multiplied excitons from singlet fission to be selectively extracted . <p> The end result , when pairing this molybdenum-based complex with tetracene-based materials in solution , allowed the team to harvest energy at quantum yields of around 130 per cent . <p> This means that approximately 1.3 molybdenum-based metal complexes were excited per photon absorbed , exceeding the conventional 100 per cent limit and indicating that the system generated and harvested more energy carriers than photons received . <p> The researchers hope that their work can help establish a new design strategy for exciton amplification , though they recognise their current experiments are only at the proof-of-concept stage . The goal is to bring the two types of materials together in the solid state and are aiming for efficient energy transfer and eventual integration into working solar cells . <p> Joshua S.
